rv.q: But intermittent gorgeousness is not, for me, a sufficient substitute for substance.
Mileage will vary on how hard such sentiments hit.

While Sarnak’s music — awash with yearning that drowns out its less precise imagery — and this cast’s performances provide The Lonely Few with rock-operatic charge, the musical itself gets sluggish, and that’s largely because Bonds’s book is really predictable.
Malloy’s masterwork is a triumph in that it touches us so deeply as it entertains.
Three Houses is an elegant, psychologically fertile theatrical experience with a score that strives to make beautiful sense out of a harrowing mass experience.
I was simply thrilled to see a writer shoot for the moon and pretty much get there.
Loaded with a dynamite ensemble, Three Houses proves to be another nerve-striking, unmissable Dave Malloy musical.
If there are instances in which Malloy's script and score wrestle with too many ideas, there are several musical moments that are positively ravishing.
Like these other shows ,“Three Houses” is surely meant to charm, but it more often struck me as peculiar or pointless.
But the disparate pieces never bundle into something fully legible, and Malloy’s sinewy music drifts away too wispily to cohere: As drama, this is, perhaps, closest to a house of straw.
By the time Beckett is attempting to build a fortress in his squalid bachelor pad, things have become ho-hum.
But Three Houses is hemmed in by its limitations, talking and singing constantly without saying very much at all.
“Three Houses” is an intriguing cautionary tale about the vicissitudes of the human condition and well worth seeing.

cn.t: Malloy's pandemic-themed musical triptych earns praise for its inventive staging, haunting score, and imaginative design, though critics are mixed on whether audiences are ready to revisit Covid isolation through song.
